summary:
NextCrop is an app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that hold up as the climate changes. The farmer answers five plain questions: where the field is, what they grow now, where their water comes from, their soil type, and which goals matter most. The challenge brief lists six goals: water use, animal feed, nitrogen fixing, erosion, soil organic matter and market value.

Field Shift fills in the rest from NASA and partner Earth observations. These include NASA POWER weather, GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, MODIS, Landsat, Sentinel-2 vegetation indices and GRACE groundwater. From them it works out each field's wet months, dry spells, frost, heat stress and long-term trends.

A rule-based model, following published rotation research (ROTOR; Fenz et al. 2023), tests thousands of possible rotations. It returns the farmer's current rotation and two alternatives, each with plain-language benefits, risks and things to check locally. We chose rules over a black box so that every recommendation can be traced and trusted.

This matters because rotation decisions shape soil health, water use and income for years. Field Shift gives every farmer satellite-informed advice for free.
details:
What it does and how it works

Field Shift helps a farmer answer one hard question: given what the climate is actually doing to my field, what should I grow next and why?

The farmer defines a field (by dropping coordinates on a map, or using the built-in Rothamsted Broadbalk demo field) and enters their current crop rotation, soil type, water source, and priorities (for example: protect soil, maximise income, cut fertiliser). From there:

  1. We pull real NASA climate data for that exact point. Field Shift fetches 20+ years of NASA POWER daily data for the field's coordinates (keyless, no account needed) and builds a farm climate profile — rainfall totals, wet and dry months, frost windows, growing-season temperature, and multi-year heat and drought trends.
  2. A transparent agronomy engine scores rotations. A rule-based model evaluates crop rotations across nine agronomy "buckets" (soil, water, fertility, forage, organic matter, crop sequence, income, climate, and resilience to change), using FAO EcoCrop climate envelopes for 25 UK crops and a crop-successor matrix (how well crop B follows crop A). The buckets are weighted by the farmer's own stated priorities.
  3. It returns a comparison, not a single verdict. The farmer sees their current rotation alongside a recommended option and an alternative — each one explained in plain language: the benefits, the risks, the reasoning, the data gaps, and what still needs a local expert to confirm. Ranking stays inside the engine; the interface shows plans and calendars, not raw scores.
  4. It is honest about uncertainty. NASA satellite rainfall is checked against a physical ground rain gauge at Rothamsted (recording continuously since 1853). Where the satellite and the ground disagree, we show the farmer the gap instead of hiding it.

Under the hood, two independent engines share one API and interface: a global field engine (Google Earth Engine + NASA POWER, for field-scale NDVI and suitability anywhere on Earth) and a UK rotation model (the rule-based scoring engine over 25 crops). A FastAPI layer wraps both; it never re-implements their logic.

Benefits

  • Grounded in real, local, long-term data — not generic regional advice. Every recommendation is tied to 20+ years of climate at the farmer's own coordinates.
  • Explainable by design. A farmer can read exactly why one rotation beat another, rather than trusting a black box.
  • Free and accessible. The core model and its demo field need no API keys or paid services; NASA POWER is open and keyless.
  • Respects the farmer's goals. The same field produces different recommendations depending on whether the farmer prioritises income, soil health, or reduced inputs.
  • Honest about its limits, so it earns trust instead of overpromising.

Intended impact

Climate change is making the "grow what we grew last year" habit riskier each season. Field Shift turns decades of NASA Earth-observation data into a practical, field-specific planning tool that helps farmers adapt rotations to a shifting climate — improving soil health, reducing wasted fertiliser and water, and supporting more resilient yields. It is deliberately advisory: it supports a farmer's or agronomist's judgment rather than replacing it, keeping a human expert in the loop for the decisions that matter.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Data sources: NASA POWER (daily climate, MERRA-2 lineage), Google Earth Engine (field-scale NDVI), FAO EcoCrop (crop climate envelopes), a crop-successor matrix (Fenz et al. 2023 + UK agronomy), and the Rothamsted electronic rain-gauge archive (ground-truth, CC BY 4.0).
  • Core engines: Python 3.12 — plain Python packages for the field engine and the UK rotation model, plus reproducible data-build scripts (raw NASA/EcoCrop downloads → clean processed tables).
  • API layer: FastAPI.
  • Frontend: Next.js / React (TypeScript), Node 20+. (An earlier Streamlit app remains as a legacy interface.)
  • Quality & tooling: pytest test suite (rule engine, input bridge, Earth Engine services, ET₀ maths, API), Ruff linting, TypeScript type-checking.
  • Deployment: Docker / docker-compose, Render, Vercel, and Streamlit Community Cloud configs — the UK model and its demo field run with no secrets in every deploy mode.
  • Hardware: none custom — it runs on commodity cloud/laptop hardware; all "sensing" comes from existing NASA satellites and the Rothamsted ground station.

How the project is creative

  • It compares instead of commanding. Most tools hand down one answer; Field Shift shows the current, recommended, and alternative rotations side by side, each explained — treating the farmer as a decision-maker, not a button-pusher.
  • It makes uncertainty a feature, not a flaw. We validated NASA satellite rainfall against 300 months of a real ground gauge (correlation 0.87, mean bias −1.4%, but a −22% underestimate in the wettest 10% of months) and surface that gap in the interface — a transparency move that's unusual in consumer-facing climate tools.
  • It fuses satellite data with centuries-old ground truth — pairing modern NASA Earth observation with a rain record kept since 1853.
  • A rule-based, readable engine was a deliberate creative choice over an opaque machine-learning model, so every recommendation can be explained and trusted.

Factors the team considered

  • Trust over cleverness — explainability and honesty about data gaps were prioritised, because a farmer won't act on advice they can't understand.
  • Scope and honesty — the rotation rules are UK-specific, so coordinates outside the UK are rejected rather than scored on a climate the model wasn't built for.
  • What satellites can and can't see — below-surface facts (like soil mineral nitrogen) are entered by the farmer, not pretended to be sensed from space; satellite resolution (a ~0.5° grid cell, not a point) is disclosed, not glossed over.
  • Accessibility — keyless data and a no-secrets demo mode so anyone can run and evaluate it.
  • Human-in-the-loop safety — the tool is explicitly advisory, with "needs a local expert" checks attached to its recommendations.
